segments.say: So let's slow down now. There's nothing more to learn tonight, and nothing you need to remember. From here, the idea is simply to rest, and to let the voice in your head grow a little quieter, a little kinder, and a little slower, one small step at a time.

If you haven't already, find a position that feels easy. Let your head be heavy on the pillow. Let your hands rest wherever they want to rest. You don't need to lie perfectly still, and you don't need to do this correctly. There's no correct way. There's only your way, tonight.

Notice your breathing, without changing it. The air comes in, and the air goes out. In, and out. If your mind wanders, that's fine. It's what minds do. When you notice it has wandered, you can just come back to the breath, the way you'd come back to a book after looking up for a moment.

For the next few minutes, there is nothing to fix, nothing to solve and nothing to decide. All of those things will still be there in the morning, when you have more energy for them. For now, your only job is to listen, and even that is optional.
Earlier we said that for many people the inner voice gets louder at night. Let's think about that gently for a moment.

show.title: Why the voice gets loud at night

segments.say: During the day, your attention is full. There are voices around you, messages, tasks and noise. In a dark, quiet room, there's nothing else to listen to, so the inner voice has the whole stage. And it often fills that stage with unfinished business: the email you didn't send, the call you need to make, the thing you forgot to buy.

It may help to think of that voice as a slightly anxious assistant. It's not trying to keep you awake. It's trying to make sure nothing important gets lost. The trouble is that it doesn't know you've heard it. So it keeps repeating itself, like someone who isn't sure their message got through.
There's a small study that offers a very practical way to reassure that assistant.

In 2018, Michael Scullin and his colleagues at Baylor University in Texas published a study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. Fifty seven young adults spent a night in a sleep laboratory. Before lights out, they spent five minutes writing. Half wrote a list of the things they needed to do in the next few days. The other half wrote about tasks they had already completed.

show.what: Writing a to-do list for 5 minutes before bed helped people fall asleep faster

segments.say: The people who wrote a to-do list fell asleep faster than those who wrote about finished tasks. And among the to-do writers, those who wrote more specific lists tended to fall asleep faster still. It's one small study, and the researchers said it needed repeating with more people, but the idea is easy to try.

show.title: Volunteers in the sleep lab
show.label: five minutes of writing before lights out (Scullin et al., 2018)

segments.say: One possible reason is that writing the list tells the anxious assistant, message received. The tasks are safely stored on paper, so the voice doesn't have to keep holding them up in the dark. You've moved them from your head to the page.

If you have a notebook nearby, you could do this tomorrow night before you turn out the light. For tonight, we'll do a gentler version, entirely in your head. You don't need to sit up or open your eyes. We'll simply set things down, one at a time.
Let's try it now, slowly. I'll make a few suggestions, and you can let your inner voice answer, or not.

Think of one thing you need to do tomorrow. Just one. It might be small, like buying bread, or bigger, like a conversation you've been putting off. Let your inner voice say it once, simply. Bread. Or, call my sister. And then imagine placing it on a shelf, where it will wait for you until morning.

Now, if there's another thing, let it come. Name it once. And place it on the shelf next to the first. You don't need to plan how you'll do it. You don't need to worry about whether you'll manage. You're only telling yourself, I know about this, and it's safe here until tomorrow.

If more things come, you can put them all on the shelf, one by one. And if your inner voice wants to start working on any of them, you can say to it, quietly, thank you, not now. Tomorrow. It has done its job. It has reminded you. Now it can rest.

Those three little words can be a kind of lullaby for the anxious assistant. Thank you, because it was trying to help. Not now, because now is for rest. And tomorrow, because the shelf will still be there when the light comes back.

show.title: A little phrase for the night

segments.say: Now let's notice how the inner voice is speaking. Not what it's saying, but how it sounds.

During the day, your inner voice may race, jumping from thought to thought. At night, you can invite it to slow down. Imagine that it's walking instead of running. Each word a little further from the next. Each thought given its own space, like stepping stones across a quiet stream.

Remember how inner speech can be expanded or condensed? At night, you might let it become as condensed as it likes. Not full sentences, just a word here and there. Warm. Heavy. Soft. Quiet. There's no need to explain anything to yourself. You already know what you mean.

And remember, too, that some people describe their thoughts as words without sound. You might let your own inner voice become a little like that tonight. Quieter and quieter, until the words are hardly words at all, just a gentle sense of meaning, drifting past.

If it helps, you can borrow a few resting words. Warm. Heavy. Soft. Slow. Safe. You don't need to say them in order, and you don't need to say them at all. They're just there, like cushions, in case your mind wants something soft to lean on.

Come back to the breath for a moment. The air comes in, cool. The air goes out, a little warmer. You don't need to make it deeper or slower. It's already doing exactly what it needs to do, without any help from you.

In a little while, we'll try another small idea from the research we met earlier, putting a feeling into a word. For now, just rest here with your shelf of tomorrow's things, safely set down, and your breath coming and going on its own.
